title: Look at the game, not the tests
dek: A new benchmark has coding agents build whole 3D browser games, and the ones that checked the running game made the games people voted for. Plus PostgreSQL 19, a hypothesis log for stuck agents, and night lighting from one dither pattern.

theme.mood: a Friday about checking the thing itself

tldr.text: In **3D GameDev Arena**, coding agents built 108 browser games. Two tied on code tests, yet people preferred one's games about twice as often; it debugged on real builds and live browser checks.
**PostgreSQL 19** is out: get-or-create in one statement, read-your-writes on replicas with `WAIT FOR LSN`, and table cleanup that no longer locks the table.
A hardware hacker's agent workflow: keep every hypothesis in a CSV, give each one experiment, and write findings to Markdown so they survive a context reset.
ArtStation's marketplace stops taking orders on December 18 and hands its sellers to Gumroad; listings must be confirmed by hand before they go live.
GlagStone lights a whole 1-bit town at night with one 8 by 8 dither pattern, and Free Lives explains why one good number was not enough to greenlight Dressmaker.

blocks.title: Coding agents built 108 browser games. The ones that played them won
blocks.gist: Coding agents built complete 3D browser games from a written brief, and people voted on the results. Passing code tests did not predict the votes; agents that ran and checked the real game made the games people preferred.
blocks.background: Coding agents are usually tested on small fixes in existing projects. Building a whole game from nothing takes hundreds of steps, and a game can pass every test and still be unpleasant to play.
blocks.takeaway: Two agents scored the same on code tests, yet people chose one's games about twice as often. The difference was where they spent their debugging: on type checks and unit tests, or on full builds and the game running in a browser.
body: **3D GameDev Arena**, from researchers at Fudan University, the Shanghai Innovation Institute and Shanghai Jiao Tong University, gives an agent a text spec and reference images for one of 108 games across 14 genres, from lane runners to shooters. An automated plan, build, test and repair loop runs until the game is done. A typical build took about 1,000 model calls; the longest took 14,407 calls and 2.13 billion tokens and made 608 assets.

Each game is scored three ways: automated checks that the required features work, an agent that plays planned key moments and judges how the game looks and plays, and blind head-to-head votes from people in a public arena. Kimi K3 matched GPT-6 Astra on the feature checks (59.8 against 59.4 of 100) but won only 27.4% of human votes, against 66.2%.

The authors trace the gap to debugging habits. Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3 spent about 63% of their debugging on static checks that never draw a frame. The two Codex setups spent about 90% on full builds, integration tests and live browser checks. Agents were better at menus and transitions than at responsive 3D controls.
blocks.why: If an agent's only definition of done is green tests, it can ship a game that compiles and plays badly. Making it build, run and look at the result is the habit that separated the best entries here.
blocks.forYou: The browser games' agent setup should require a production build and a headless look at the running page before anything counts as done; the same applies to the Unreal plugins' demo maps through automated PIE runs.

stat.label: of human votes won by an agent that tied on code tests

image.alt: Two agent-built lane runners for the same task. Left, codex-gpt-6.1-sol: a bright cartoon runner on rails with coins and a jump prompt. Right, zcode-glm-5.3: a photographic rail yard with a tutorial panel over the track.
image.credit: Bai, Jian, Yan et al., arXiv (labels added)

terms.def: Checks that read the code without running the game, such as a type checker or unit tests.
Tests that run several parts of the program together, closer to how it really runs.
The chunks of text a language model reads and writes; usage is billed by them.

deep: Scores out of 100 (functional, 3D presentation, playability, Bradley-Terry vote score, raw win rate): codex-gpt-6.1-sol 64.7, 57.8, 68.4, 69.11, 62.8%; codex-gpt-6-astra 59.4, 58.5, 69.5, 69.24, 66.2%; kimi-k3 59.8, 42.3, 64.9, 25.86, 27.4%; zcode-glm-5.3 51.2, 23.5, 54.9, 35.78, 30.6%.

Median per game: 692 to 1,067 tool calls and 70.1 to 202.1 million tokens, most of it cached context re-read on every call. In the paper's worked example on the lane runner task, the judge faults zcode-glm-5.3 for a tutorial panel that keeps covering the runner and the track. arXiv preprint 2611.24073, submitted November 18, 2026; no code repository is linked.

blocks.title: How much debugging went to checks that never run the game
blocks.gist: The two agents whose games people liked least spent most of their debugging on code checks; the two most liked spent under an eighth of it there and the rest on builds and live play.
blocks.intro: Share of each agent's debugging spent on type checks and unit tests alone, from 3D GameDev Arena.
blocks.note: Human vote scores in the same order: 25.86, 35.78, 69.24, 69.11. The paper's own measurements; a correlation across four setups, not a controlled test.
blocks.why: Where an agent spends its checking time is something you can set in its instructions today.
blocks.forYou: Worth a look at which commands the agent actually runs in the three.js projects: if it is mostly tsc and vitest, add a build and a browser check.

terms.def: Small automated tests that check one function or piece of code on its own.

blocks.title: A stuck agent needs a lab notebook, not another guess
blocks.gist: A hardware hacker who uses agents to reverse engineer cameras, synths and printers shares the loop that stops them guessing in circles: one written hypothesis, one experiment, one recorded result at a time.
blocks.intro: The loop, from a hardware hacker's write-up.

steps.title: Write findings to Markdown
steps.text: The agent keeps notes in files, so what it learned survives a context reset or a handoff to another agent.

steps.title: Log the hypothesis
steps.text: Each idea about how the system works goes into a CSV table on disk before anything is tried.

steps.title: Design one experiment
steps.text: A probe, a log line or a test that settles that one hypothesis either way.

steps.title: Record, then repeat
steps.text: Write the result in the table and pick the next hypothesis. The author calls this skill crucial.

blocks.why: Agents fail on hard bugs by retrying the same idea. A written record of what was ruled out turns that into progress you can read.
blocks.forYou: This is today's Try this: add it as a skill for the Unreal plugin bugs that only show up in packaged builds.

terms.def: Work out how a device or program works from the outside, without its source code or documentation.
When an agent's working memory is cleared or summarized, so it loses details it had seen.

deep: From a write-up that reached 302 points on Hacker News; the author used it to build custom firmware for several synthesizers and map the protocols of two Sony cameras. Tools named: DeepSeek v4.1 Flash in its own harness (sometimes Codex), Ghidra through an MCP bridge, radare2, Python with uv for probes, and Rust for the final hacks because its compiler gives fast feedback. Two more skills: one that has the agent ask up to five crucial questions one at a time, and one that documents the reverse engineering tools, without which the author says agents give up too early. Posted November 18, 2026.

blocks.title: A software factory that merged 238 agent pull requests in a week
blocks.gist: Mastra open-sourced the board its own team uses to hand work to coding agents from Slack. Last week the agents opened and merged 238 pull requests, beside 630 merged by people.
blocks.background: Mastra is an open-source TypeScript framework for building AI agents, downloaded close to 4 million times a week.
blocks.intro: The stages a task moves through on the board. People can step in at each one.

nodes.label: Triage
nodes.note: A request from Slack or GitHub becomes a card

nodes.label: Plan
nodes.note: The team is moving toward skipping this step

nodes.label: Build
nodes.note: A coding agent works in a cloud sandbox

nodes.label: Review
nodes.note: Pull request comments feed back into the session

nodes.label: Ship
nodes.note: Merged under the team's GitHub App

blocks.caption: Team-reported numbers. Hacker News commenters questioned whether a factory is more than agents working through ordinary issues, and worried about losing the feel of the product.
blocks.why: This is one of the first agent factories released with a count of what it merged in production, and it runs on your own infrastructure.
blocks.forYou: The board and stages map closely onto the routines and subagents already in use; worth reading how review comments feed back into a running session.

terms.def: Proposed code changes submitted for review before they are merged.
An isolated computer where an agent can run code without touching anything else.

deep: Install with `npm create factory`; a hosted version is also offered. Built on Mastra's durable agents, conversational memory, a Markdown wiki with citations, and signals that pass PR comments into sessions. The default coding harness is mastracode, with Claude Code and Codex support planned. The team closed its repository to outside pull requests and now asks for detailed reproductions instead.

blocks.title: Messy code costs agents more tokens
blocks.gist: Adam Tornhill of CodeScene says agents use far fewer tokens on clean code, and fix far more problems when a tool tells them where the problems are.

stats.label: fewer tokens needed on healthy code
of issues an agent fixes alone in weaker code, at best

body: Speaker's own figures from a GOTO Copenhagen talk, reported by InfoQ; CodeScene sells the code health tool.
blocks.why: Refactoring is now also a way to cut your agent bill, and a quality metric the agent can query works as a guardrail.
blocks.forYou: A lint or complexity report exposed as an MCP tool is cheap to try on the oldest SaaS backend.

terms.def: A small program that offers tools or data to an AI agent through a standard protocol.

deep: Tornhill also cites a study of over 1,000 open-source projects in which AI velocity gains were cancelled by rising complexity after about two months, an average code health score of 5.15, and 9.5 as the point where code becomes AI-friendly.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL 19: everyday wins and a few upgrade checks
blocks.gist: The new version of the most popular open-source database makes common app patterns one statement, lets apps read their own writes from a copy of the database, and cleans tables without locking them.
blocks.name: PostgreSQL 19
blocks.what: The yearly major release, out November 19, about two months later than usual.
body: Simon Willison links the delay to a wave of AI-reported security fixes. His favourite feature lets a read replica wait until it has caught up with a write you just made, so a user never sees stale data after saving.

facts.v: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT` returns the existing row
JIT now off; md5 logins warn

blocks.why: Get-or-create and replica reads are patterns most web apps hand-roll today. Hosted Postgres providers will roll it out on their own schedule.
blocks.forYou: Get-or-create and REPACK matter for the Supabase projects; check whether any still use md5 passwords before Supabase offers 19.

terms.def: A copy of the database that follows the main one and serves reads to spread the load.
Just-in-time compilation: turning a query into machine code while it runs, which only pays off for big queries.

deep: Also new: `IGNORE NULLS` for lead, lag and the value window functions, JSON output from `COPY`, the pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice extensions to pin a query plan without code changes, parallel index vacuuming, and logical replication that raises the WAL level by itself. RADIUS authentication is removed, and `io_workers` becomes `io_min_workers` and `io_max_workers`. With LZ4 built in, the default TOAST compression is now lz4.

blocks.title: Gemini loads a tool's details only when it needs the tool
blocks.gist: Google's Gemini API can now hold back the full description of rarely used tools and fetch it mid-request, so an app with hundreds of tools sends far less text on every call.
blocks.intro: Mark a tool `defer_loading`; the model still sees its name and one-line description and asks for the rest when needed. From Google's announcement, trimmed.
blocks.code:
tools = [
   {"type": "tool_search"},
   {
       "type": "function",
       "name": "issue_refund",
       "description": "Refund an order to the original payment method.",
       "defer_loading": True,
       "parameters": {"type": "object", ...},
   },
   # ... 50+ other deferred functions
]
interaction = client.interactions.create(
   model="gemini-4-hydrogen",
   input="Order A-1042 arrived damaged. Please refund 40 dollars.",
   tools=tools,
)
explain: Loaded schemas join the conversation later, so the start of the prompt stays the same and keeps hitting the cache.
Setting `defer_loading` on an MCP server defers all of its tools. No extra charge; Google gives no savings figures and says to measure on your own traffic.
blocks.why: Tool lists are a hidden cost in every agent call. Deferring them while keeping the prompt cache-friendly is becoming a standard pattern across providers.
blocks.forYou: Any SaaS feature that calls Gemini with a long tool list is a candidate; keep the two or three most used tools loaded.

terms.def: The formal description of a tool's inputs that the model needs before it can call it.

deep: In preview in the Interactions API for Gemini 3.6 and later. For your own registry or permission checks, declare `tool_search` with `"execution": "client"` and return matching schemas yourself, at the cost of one extra round trip per search. Announced November 19, 2026.

sources.label: Google: Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API

blocks.title: Claude Code: a check-up for your setup, and two changed defaults
blocks.gist: Claude Code's last three releases add a command that finds broken parts of your setup and one place to stop background loops, and change how code review and failed hooks behave.

items.title: /status finds what is broken
items.text: It now lists broken agent, skill and command files, hook matchers that never match and permission settings that are ignored. Run it once and fix the list.

items.title: /tasks shows loops and schedules
items.text: Scheduled tasks, loop wakeups, the goal and forks appear in one list, and x stops one after asking. Tasks saved by older versions may need scheduling again.

items.title: Failed hooks no longer block in Code Mode
items.text: A PreToolUse hook that errors now lets the tool call through, as outside Code Mode. Hooks that must stop an action need onFailure set to block.

items.title: /code-review covers the whole branch
items.text: With no target it reviews the branch against the default branch. The automatic retry at the output token limit is also gone.

blocks.why: Safety hooks that quietly stop blocking are the change to check first if you rely on hooks to guard what an agent may do.
blocks.forYou: Run /status on each project, and add onFailure block to any guard hook that must hold in Code Mode.

terms.def: A script the tool runs automatically before or after an action, for example to check or block it.
A Claude Code mode where the model writes small scripts that call its tools, instead of calling them one at a time.

deep: Behind a gateway whose model accepts fewer output tokens, set `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` to that limit. Version 2.1.327 also adds `claude mcp add-json <name> -`, which reads a server's JSON from stdin so tokens stay out of shell history, and 2.1.329's trust dialog says where a folder's hooks are declared.

blocks.title: One 8 by 8 pattern lights a whole 1-bit town at night
blocks.gist: GlagStone, a black and white city builder styled after 1980s Macintosh games, does its night lighting, lamplight, water and weather with a single repeating grid of thresholds that decides which pixels turn black.
blocks.plain: Each pixel is compared with a number from a small repeating grid; as the scene darkens, more pixels fall below their number and go black, so light fades in an even, readable pattern.

image.alt: A 1-bit black and white island town at night, with a lighthouse beam sweeping in a wide white wedge across dark dithered roofs, and a building menu on the right.

body: The four-person team builds in LÖVE, a free Lua game framework, with their own editor for dialogue and events. Light sources live on separate layers: a lantern leaves a pale pool that thins into black, and the lighthouse beam sweeps the town and reveals roofs that were hidden a moment before. The team previously shipped on the Playdate handheld.
blocks.why: A two-color look usually rules out smooth lighting. Ordered dithering gives it back with one comparison per pixel, cheap enough for any engine or a web shader.
blocks.forYou: A dither threshold pass is a small three.js post effect; it could give a browser game a distinct look at almost no cost.

terms.def: Faking shades of grey with a pattern of only black and white pixels.
A free framework for making 2D games in the Lua programming language.

blocks.title: Why one good number was not enough to greenlight Dressmaker
blocks.gist: Free Lives' early numbers for its dressmaking game looked weak, so the studio ran a second test on social media before committing; the game became a hit, and the studio changed how it reads early data.
blocks.quote: We now know that you need multiple corroborating signals in order to trust that a project has appeal.
blocks.speaker: Ruan Rothman
blocks.context: Dressmaker's free prototype got about 10,000 itch.io downloads in its first month, low for the studio. An earlier prototype passed 100,000 downloads and then underperformed on Steam. A second push on Instagram and TikTok found an audience, so the team went ahead with a limited scope. The game now has thousands of overwhelmingly positive Steam reviews.
blocks.why: Prototype downloads, social views and creator videos each mislead on their own. Look for several that agree before committing a year to a game.
blocks.forYou: Before the next plugin or game idea gets full scope, set two or three independent signals to watch, not one.

blocks.title: A record year of games sent to Godot's showreel
blocks.gist: The free, open-source Godot engine received more submissions than ever for its yearly showreel of games made with it, and will change how entries are picked next year.

stats.label: games and projects submitted, a record

body: Next year entries that break the rules are removed first, then voting opens to all development fund members and contributors. This year's reel includes Slay the Spire 2.
blocks.why: Submission counts are a rough gauge of how many teams ship with an engine; Godot's keeps growing.
blocks.forYou: Useful context for where browser and mobile tooling effort is going outside Unreal.

learn.question: What is ordered dithering?
learn.answer: A way to show shades with only black and white pixels: each pixel's brightness is compared with a number from a small repeating grid, and it turns white only if it beats that number.
learn.analogy: Like a stadium card stunt: each seat has its own rule for when to raise a white card, so as the signal grows, more seats join in an even pattern and the crowd shows a smooth shade.
body: The grid is called a Bayer matrix. An 8 by 8 version holds the numbers 0 to 63 arranged so that neighbouring cells are far apart in value. Tiled across the screen, it means a mid grey becomes an even checker of black and white, not a blob. Darken the scene and pixels drop out in a stable order, so a fading light looks smooth even at two colors.

It was standard on early displays and printers with few colors, and it is back as a look: GlagStone uses one 8 by 8 pattern for night, lamplight, water and weather. In a shader it is one texture lookup and one comparison per pixel, so it runs anywhere.

nodes.label: Light
nodes.note: How bright this pixel should be, 0 to 1

nodes.label: Grid
nodes.note: The Bayer value at this pixel's spot in the 8 by 8 tile

nodes.label: Test
nodes.note: Is brightness above the grid value?

diagram.caption: One comparison per pixel. Lowering the light at dusk turns more pixels black in a fixed, even order.

terms.def: A small square grid of threshold numbers, ordered so that the pattern it makes stays even at every shade.
A small program that runs on the graphics card to work out the color of each pixel.

tryThis.title: Give your agent a hypothesis log for bugs it cannot crack
tryThis.gist: A small skill that makes the agent write down each idea and test it once, so a stuck session turns into a list of ruled-out causes instead of the same retry.
tryThis.needs: Claude Code (or any agent that reads skills) and a bug the agent has already failed to fix.

steps.title: Create the skill
steps.text: Add a folder .claude/skills/hypothesis-debugging with the SKILL.md below. The CSV columns are a starting point; the author's own skill is on GitHub.

steps.title: Point the agent at the stuck bug
steps.text: Ask it to use the hypothesis-debugging skill and keep its notes in Markdown files, as the source recommends, so they survive a context reset.

steps.title: Read the table, not the transcript
steps.text: After a few rounds, open the CSV. Each row should be a different idea with a concrete experiment and a result.

steps.title: Add questions if it stalls
steps.text: The author also asks the agent for up to five crucial questions, one at a time, when human knowledge would help.

code.code:
---
name: hypothesis-debugging
description: Use when a bug or unknown behaviour survives two fix attempts.
---
Keep a table at notes/hypotheses.csv with columns:
id,hypothesis,experiment,result,status

1. Write one hypothesis about the cause.
2. Design one experiment (a probe, a log line, a test)
   that proves or disproves it.
3. Run it, record the result, mark it confirmed or rejected.
4. Add what you learned to notes/findings.md.
5. Pick the next hypothesis. Never retry a rejected one
   without new evidence.

tryThis.check: The CSV fills with distinct hypotheses and recorded results, the agent stops repeating the same fix, and notes/findings.md explains the cause once it is found.
tryThis.forYou: Try it on the next Unreal plugin bug that only reproduces in a packaged build, where agents tend to guess.

terms.def: A folder of instructions an agent loads when a task matches its description.

lab.title: When Agents Play Differently: Localizing Human-Agent Behavioral Divergence with Conditional Distributional Testing
lab.headline: A playtest bot can match players on win rate and still play nothing like them
lab.authors: Oleg Smirnov, John Pertoft, Sara Karimi (King AI Labs, Microsoft Gaming; KTH Royal Institute of Technology)
lab.problem: Studios use bots to playtest levels before players see them, and check the bots against people by comparing averages like win rate. That can hide where a bot plays differently.
lab.idea: Split play into cells by game mode and difficulty, compare the whole spread of per-move measures (score per move, cascades per move) between bots and humans in each cell, then search for the rules that describe where they differ, with false-alarm control.
lab.result: On about 110,000 human sessions of a commercial match-3 game and 5,000 per bot, win and loss added little beyond averages. In cascades per move, the cloned bot differed most in Chain mode and the hint bot in harder Clear and Route levels. In a synthetic check, false discoveries were 0.004 against 0.216 for an averages-only method.
lab.useIt: If a bot tunes your difficulty, log per-move measures and compare them with real players per mode and level, not just overall win rate; trust the bot only where it matches.
lab.forYou: Relevant for any AI playtester in the browser games: check it per level type before trusting its difficulty readings.

image.alt: Two heatmaps of divergence between bots and humans across 24 cells of game mode and difficulty, for score per move and cascades per move; darker cells mark bigger differences.

note: Sparks run six, but Farcall's signal is small. The marble carving write-up is from October and reached Hacker News this week. OpenAI's posts and the ArtStation announcement refused fetches, so the seller FAQ is the source there.
